To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

PNI is associated with lethal prostate cancers in two independent cohorts of untreated and treated patients, suggesting that PNI creates a microenvironment conducive to cancer aggressiveness and metastasis.
perineural tumor invasion is an independent predictor of lethal prostate cancer, even after adjustment for clinical and pathologic factors.

(i) perineural invasion was associated with aggressive prostate cancer in both untreated and treated cohorts (ii) perineural invasive tumors had higher tumor angiogenesis and were more common in high grade tumors, but not tumor cell proliferation or apoptosis, and (iii) in the U.S. cohort, perineural invasion predicted lethal prostate cancer after adjustment for age and tumor grade.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of perineural invasion in prostate cancer progression.
the development of prostate cancer, its progression to metastatic disease, and the role of inflammation in the development of these diseases.
the molecular mechanisms underlying the metastatic process in prostate cancer.

PNI has a strong association with aggressive prostate cancer and is an important prognostic factor for prostate cancer.
PNI in prostate tumors is associated with a higher risk of aggressive disease, but this association is confounded by the presence of high Gleason grade.
PNI is associated with aggressive prostate cancer, and is associated with a worse prognosis, independent of clinical parameters.

the association between perineural invasion and lethal prostate cancer was stronger in men who underwent watch and wait than in those who underwent radical prostatectomy (i.e. in men who were less likely to be treated with androgen deprivation therapy).
